quests.instruction: Say it aloud: which words join up?
quests.hint: Degree phrases are said very fast. Which two words get squashed into one beat?
quests.explanation: 'Kind of' is often squeezed into one beat, even 'kinda'. The /d/ of 'kind' lands on the weak /əv/, and the pair behaves like a single word placed before 'tired'.
quests.flowRule: Weak Function Words: Short grammar words such as a, an, of, at, and, or and it are normally unstressed and begin with a vowel sound, so they attach to the word before them.

quests.instruction: Which pair would a fluent speaker say in one breath?
quests.hint: 'Really quite' sounds close, but check what each second word begins with.
quests.explanation: Both 'really quite' and 'quite expensive' might seem to link, but only one does. 'Really' ends in a vowel and 'quite' starts with /k/, so there is nothing to join. 'Quite' ends in /t/ and 'expensive' starts with a vowel, so the /t/ lands on it.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which pair is spoken continuously?
quests.hint: Agreeing with someone. Which word ending in a cluster runs into a weak vowel?
quests.explanation: 'About' starts with a weak vowel, so the /z/ of 'sounds' slides over it and you hear one phrase. 'About right' cannot link: /t/ + /r/.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which boundary has no pause?
quests.hint: Telling the time: one clock word ends in a consonant cluster before a number that starts with a vowel.
quests.explanation: Time phrases get compressed. The final /t/ of 'past' flows into the /eɪ/ of 'eight', so the clock reading sounds like one unit.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which words melt together when you say this naturally?
quests.hint: Schedule talk is fast. Which verb ends in a hushing sound before a small word?
quests.explanation: 'Finish' ends in /ʃ/ and 'at' is a weak /ət/, so the hush flows straight into it, with the stress on 'fin' and 'nine'. 'At nine' does not link, because /t/ meets /n/.
quests.flowRule: Weak Function Words: Short grammar words such as a, an, of, at, and, or and it are normally unstressed and begin with a vowel sound, so they attach to the word before them.

quests.instruction: Which two words run together?
quests.hint: Look at the verb right after 'I'. What is its last sound and what follows?
quests.explanation: 'Until' starts with /ʌ/, so the /k/ of 'work' has something to land on. 'Until ten' cannot link, because /l/ meets /t/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Identify the linked pair
quests.hint: Tech instructions often end with a verb plus a short particle. Where does the verb's last sound go?
quests.explanation: 'Log in' and 'login' sound almost the same because the /g/ is released straight into the vowel. Leave a gap and it sounds like two unrelated words.
quests.flowRule: Phrasal verbs: In a verb plus particle (log in, fill out, look up), the particle usually starts with a vowel, so the two words are spoken as one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: Read the line aloud and join the right pair
quests.hint: Forms and offices: a verb followed by a particle. Check the sound at the end of the verb.
quests.explanation: In a phrasal verb the particle is a tail. The /l/ of 'fill' stays voiced into the /aʊ/ of 'out', which is why 'fill out' sounds like one word, not two.
quests.flowRule: Phrasal verbs: In a verb plus particle (log in, fill out, look up), the particle usually starts with a vowel, so the two words are spoken as one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: Spot the linking point
quests.hint: The first word has a consonant cluster at its end. What does it finish with when spoken quickly?
quests.explanation: Even if the /d/ of 'hand' almost vanishes in fast speech, the /n/ still carries into 'in', so you get a smooth join either way.
quests.flowRule: Phrasal verbs: In a verb plus particle (log in, fill out, look up), the particle usually starts with a vowel, so the two words are spoken as one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: Which pair would sound choppy if you stopped between them?
quests.hint: Shopping lists link too. Look at the quantity and what it measures.
quests.explanation: The final /n/ of 'dozen' is only a hum with no vowel in front of it, and it runs on into the opening vowel of 'oranges'. 'A dozen' is vowel + /d/, so no link there.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Tap the pair that sounds like one word
quests.hint: Event planning. Which verb runs into the number?
quests.explanation: Quantities attach to what you need: the /d/ of 'need' passes into the /ɪ/ of 'eleven', so the number does not stand apart from the request.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Find the pair that flows without a break
quests.hint: A statistic in conversation. The small word in the middle is tiny. Check the word before it.
quests.explanation: Statistics are spoken in chunks, and 'one in ten' is one chunk. The /n/ of 'one' links to the vowel of 'in', and then 'in ten' (/n/ + /t/) ends the chunk.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Find the pair that blends into one chunk
quests.hint: A very common casual phrase. Notice how the second word is barely audible.
quests.explanation: This is a fixed expression, so it is rarely separated. 'Thanks' ends in a hiss and 'a' is a weak /ə/; the hiss rolls on into it.
quests.flowRule: Weak Function Words: Short grammar words such as a, an, of, at, and, or and it are normally unstressed and begin with a vowel sound, so they attach to the word before them.

quests.instruction: Find the smooth connection
quests.hint: When you did not hear something, the request is short and quick. Which words get squeezed most?
quests.explanation: The /m/ of 'come' hums into the vowel of 'again', so there is no silence between them. Pausing there would sound slower and less natural.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Listen for the connected words
quests.hint: Offering to help. What does the verb meet?
quests.explanation: 'Us' is usually weak, /əs/, so the /t/ of 'get' has no gap to land in and just rolls on. 'Us some' cannot link, because /s/ meets /s/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which pair would a fluent speaker say in one breath?
quests.hint: Which word describing how often something happens ends in a buzzing sound?
quests.explanation: Frequency adverbs end in /z/, a buzzing sound you can sustain, so it does not need to stop for the vowel of 'eat'. The habit comes out as one flowing statement.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Which pair is spoken continuously?
quests.textToSpeak: I brush my teeth after breakfast
quests.hint: Daily routine. Which noun ends in a breathy sound before a vowel?
quests.explanation: The breathy /θ/ at the end of 'teeth' does not stop for the vowel in 'after'; the airflow just continues. Routine sentences are said quickly, which makes the link more obvious.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/θ/ and /ð/): The 'th' sounds at the end of a word stay in the airflow and connect to a following vowel instead of stopping.

quests.instruction: Which pair is spoken as one smooth unit?
quests.textToSpeak: I like to walk around the block
quests.hint: A word meaning 'in a circle' begins with a weak vowel. Which word comes right before it?
quests.explanation: 'Around' begins with a weak vowel, so the /k/ of 'walk' fills the gap easily. If you wait for a clear start to 'around', you will miss it.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which words melt together when you say this naturally?
quests.hint: Office tasks are said quickly. Which verb is followed by a noun that starts with a vowel?
quests.explanation: In an office this pair is so common that it works like one word. The /d/ of 'send' (sometimes very light) is released into /iː/.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which two words run together?
quests.hint: Rearranging an appointment. Which verb carries into the last word?
quests.explanation: Rescheduling talk is quick. The /t/ of 'meet' goes straight into /ɜː/, and 'can we' cannot link because /n/ meets /w/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Find the natural transition
quests.hint: Asking for help. Which word links into the noun?
quests.explanation: 'Some' is weak here (/səm/), so its /m/ is quickly released into the opening vowel of 'advice'. The stress then lands on the second syllable of 'advice'.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Read the line aloud and join the right pair
quests.hint: Check each boundary. A consonant before 'you' does not count.
quests.explanation: 'Have you' looks linked, but it is /v/ + /j/, two consonant sounds. The real vowel link is later, where the /t/ of 'got' lands on the /e/ of 'any'.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Spot the linking point
quests.hint: A shop-assistant question. Which word before the last noun ends in a consonant sound?
quests.explanation: 'Umbrella' is stressed on its second syllable, so its first vowel is weak and easy to miss. The /l/ of 'sell' fills that spot.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/l/): A word-final /l/ stays voiced and slides into the vowel of the next word, so the two words sound like one continuous stretch.

quests.instruction: Say it aloud: which words join up?
quests.hint: A contraction shortens the first word, but it still ends in a consonant.
quests.explanation: A contraction plus a short word is the most common compressed pair in shop talk. The /s/ of 'it's' runs into 'on', so 'it's on sale' is spoken in two beats.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Tap the pair that sounds like one word
quests.hint: A front-desk phrase. What does the verb end with?
quests.explanation: At a hotel desk, 'check in' is one action, and it sounds like one word. The /k/ goes straight into the vowel of 'in', which is also why the noun 'check-in' sounds identical.
quests.flowRule: Phrasal verbs: In a verb plus particle (log in, fill out, look up), the particle usually starts with a vowel, so the two words are spoken as one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: Find the pair that flows without a break
quests.hint: Airports: which noun runs into the verb?
quests.explanation: Announcements are paced so everyone can hear, but they still link. The /t/ of 'gate' is released into 'opens', and the stress sits on 'gate' and 'soon'.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which boundary has no pause?
quests.hint: Say it like a news announcement. What does the first noun's last sound meet?
quests.explanation: The verb 'is' almost never stands alone; here the /t/ of 'flight' lands on its vowel. 'Is delayed' does not link: /z/ meets /d/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Find the smooth connection
quests.hint: A phrase meaning 'met by chance'. Look at the verb's ending.
quests.explanation: 'Bumped into' is a set phrase meaning 'met by chance', so it is spoken as a single unit. The /t/ of 'bumped' attaches to 'into' and 'Sam' gets the stress.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Listen for the connected words
quests.hint: Giving directions. Ignore the first word. What ends the second?
quests.explanation: Directions are said quickly. 'Turn left' cannot link (/n/ + /l/), but 'left at' can: the /t/ goes into the weak /ət/.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Identify the linked pair
quests.hint: Two weak words meet here. Which pair is it?
quests.explanation: Two weak words together often collapse into a single beat. The /z/ of 'was' flows into the /ə/ of 'a', and the stress waits for 'good'.
